advances: The original cubic depth moment and the full-reflection cubic admit a bound in terms of the actual occupied-parity count and distinct midpoint count. This proves a dimension-uniform original-moment bound for every complete ternary support with at most two twos per point and at most a fixed multiple of the Boolean-cube cardinality in its one-step core, without any star assumption. In particular it controls the exact obstruction support of accepted fact \(49bba4c121c43db7\) for arbitrary active and neutral fields, even though its uniform core mass and coordinate-block scores tend to zero with \(m\). The general bound still deteriorates when the midpoint count divided by the parity count is unbounded; no resolution of the locked target is asserted.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The scalar inequality from accepted fact \(50c34c5bfb703ba9\) is reproved. The geometry of the application support is supplied by accepted fact \(49bba4c121c43db7\), and the one-step comparison with accepted fact \(b1d491a18220724d\) uses the explicitly matched original probabilities and halfspace depth.
proof:
All probabilities in the proof are the original probabilities in the statement. The abbreviation \(\tau_p(x)=\tau_p((x,0))\) will be used for \(x\in D\). For every \(x,y,c\in D\) with \(x+y=2c\), the affine weights give the exact identity
$$
p_c^2=\frac{\exp(-2\beta\cdot c)}{Z^2}
=\frac{\exp(-\beta\cdot x)\exp(-\beta\cdot y)}{Z^2}
=p_xp_y.
$$
The normalization map to the scalar inequality in accepted fact \(50c34c5bfb703ba9\) is to enumerate the points of one occupied parity class as \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and take its scalar entries to be \(a_i=p_{x_i}\). Their sum is the original mass of that class, rather than one. The symbols \(k,D,A,\beta,Z,p,\tau_p,M_3\) have exactly the meanings of the first assertion of accepted fact \(b1d491a18220724d\), with \(P=\operatorname{conv}(D)\) when its one-step hypotheses hold. For accepted fact \(50c34c5bfb703ba9\), they coincide when \(D=B_k\cup E\) has its stated one-step form. Neither predecessor moment theorem is being applied to a general \(D\); the finite inequality and the reflection argument are proved here.

For \(c\in D\), let
$$
R(c)=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in D,\ x\ne y\\x+y=2c}}\min(p_x,p_y).
$$
Thus \(s_p(c)=p_c+R(c)\), and \(R(c)=0\) for \(c\notin C_D\). Distinct unordered pairs reflected about \(c\) have disjoint endpoints: the partner of any endpoint \(x\) is uniquely \(2c-x\). Their endpoints are also distinct from \(c\). Every closed affine halfspace containing \((c,0)\) contains at least one endpoint of each pair. Indeed, writing the halfspace as \(\lbrace u:v\cdot u\ge t\rbrace\), if both endpoints were outside then their average \((c,0)\) would satisfy \(v\cdot(c,0)<t\), contradicting containment. The center atom and these disjoint endpoint pairs therefore give
$$
\tau_p(c)\ge p_c+\frac12R(c).
$$
This holds for every containing halfspace, including any whose boundary contains the center, and uses no rank assumption. In particular, with \(S_4=\sum_{x\in D}p_x^4\),
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_3(p)&\ge S_4,
&T(p)&\ge S_4,\\
M_3(p)&\ge\frac18\sum_{c\in C_D}p_cR(c)^3,
&T(p)&\ge\sum_{c\in C_D}p_cR(c)^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
The first row follows respectively from \(\tau_p(x)\ge p_x\) and \(s_p(x)\ge p_x\).

We rederive the scalar inequality from accepted fact \(50c34c5bfb703ba9\). For positive real numbers \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\), set
$$
K(a)=\sum_{i,j=1}^n\min(a_i,a_j)^{7/6}\max(a_i,a_j)^{1/6}.
$$
Reorder them so that \(a_1\ge\cdots\ge a_n\). For each \(i\), the \(2i-1\) ordered pairs whose largest index equals \(i\) each contribute at least \(a_i^{4/3}\). Hence \(K(a)\ge\sum_{i=1}^n i\,a_i^{4/3}\). Hölder's inequality gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i
&=\sum_{i=1}^n(i\,a_i^{4/3})^{3/4}i^{-3/4}\\
&\le\left(\sum_{i=1}^n i\,a_i^{4/3}\right)^{3/4}
\left(\sum_{i=1}^n i^{-3}\right)^{1/4}\\
&\le K(a)^{3/4}(3/2)^{1/4}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here \(\sum_{i=1}^n i^{-3}\le1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}\,dt=3/2\). Raising to the power \(4/3\) and rearranging gives
$$
K(a)\ge(2/3)^{1/3}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^{4/3}
\ge\frac34\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\right)^{4/3},
$$
where the last inequality follows from \(2/3\ge27/64\).

For each \(b\in\mathcal P_D\), put \(D_b=\lbrace x\in D:x\equiv b\pmod2\rbrace\) and \(P_b=\sum_{x\in D_b}p_x\). These \(q_D\) positive masses sum to one. Define
$$
L=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in D\\x\equiv y\pmod2}}
\min(p_x,p_y)^{7/6}\max(p_x,p_y)^{1/6}.
$$
Apply the scalar inequality to the unconditioned original probabilities in each \(D_b\), and then apply Hölder to the \(q_D\) class masses. This yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
L&\ge\frac34\sum_{b\in\mathcal P_D}P_b^{4/3},\\
1=\sum_{b\in\mathcal P_D}P_b
&\le\left(\sum_{b\in\mathcal P_D}P_b^{4/3}\right)^{3/4}q_D^{1/4},\\
L&\ge\frac34q_D^{-1/3}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The diagonal contribution to \(L\) is \(L_{\mathrm{diag}}=\sum_{x\in D}p_x^{4/3}\). Hölder with exponents \(9\) and \(9/8\) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{\mathrm{diag}}
&=\sum_{x\in D}(p_x^4)^{1/9}p_x^{8/9}\\
&\le\left(\sum_{x\in D}p_x^4\right)^{1/9}
\left(\sum_{x\in D}p_x\right)^{8/9}
=S_4^{1/9}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Let \(L_{\mathrm{off}}=L-L_{\mathrm{diag}}\). Every pair in this off-diagonal sum has its unique integral midpoint in \(C_D\), and completeness puts that midpoint in \(D\). Conversely any pair in \(R(c)\), for \(c\in C_D\), has equal parity because \(x+y=2c\). For each such pair,
\(\min(p_x,p_y)^{7/6}\max(p_x,p_y)^{1/6}
=(p_xp_y)^{1/6}\min(p_x,p_y)=p_c^{1/3}\min(p_x,p_y)\).
Consequently the exact grouping identity is
$$
L_{\mathrm{off}}=\sum_{c\in C_D}p_c^{1/3}R(c).
$$
If \(r_D>0\), Hölder on these \(r_D\) centers implies
$$
L_{\mathrm{off}}^3
\le r_D^2\sum_{c\in C_D}\bigl(p_c^{1/3}R(c)\bigr)^3
=r_D^2\sum_{c\in C_D}p_cR(c)^3.
$$
Together with the reflection estimates already proved, this gives
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac{L_{\mathrm{off}}^3}{8r_D^2},
\qquad
T(p)\ge\frac{L_{\mathrm{off}}^3}{r_D^2}.
$$

We now split into two cases. If \(S_4\ge1/(512q_D^3)\), then each of \(M_3(p)\) and \(T(p)\) is at least this quantity. Since \(\max(q_D,r_D)\ge q_D\), it is at least the claimed bound. Otherwise,
$$
S_4^{1/9}<\frac12q_D^{-1/3},
\qquad
L_{\mathrm{off}}\ge\frac34q_D^{-1/3}-S_4^{1/9}
>\frac14q_D^{-1/3}.
$$
This second case cannot occur if \(r_D=0\), because then the grouping identity gives \(L_{\mathrm{off}}=0\). For \(r_D>0\), it gives the stronger second-case bounds
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac1{512q_Dr_D^2},
\qquad
T(p)\ge\frac1{64q_Dr_D^2}.
$$
Both are at least \(1/(512q_D\max(q_D,r_D)^2)\). These two cases prove the generic assertion, including \(r_D=0\). Every step takes place in the original ambient space with the original probabilities and is valid for lower affine rank.

For the max-two corollary, the inclusion \(B_k\subseteq D\) occupies every parity class, so \(q_D=2^k\). Take distinct same-parity \(x,y\in D\), and let \(c=(x+y)/2\). It is integral, ternary, and in \(D\). A coordinate of \(c\) equals two precisely when both endpoint coordinates equal two. If two coordinates of \(c\) were two, each endpoint would already use its entire budget of at most two twos in those coordinates. Every other coordinate of each endpoint would then be binary. Same parity forces these other binary coordinates to agree, making \(x=y\), a contradiction. Thus \(c\) has at most one two, proving \(C_D\subseteq D_1\). Hence \(r_D\le|D_1|\le a2^k=a q_D\). Since \(a\ge1\), also \(\max(q_D,r_D)\le a q_D\). Substituting into the generic bound proves, for each cubic,
$$
\frac{1}{512q_D\max(q_D,r_D)^2}
\ge\frac{1}{512a^2(2^k)^3}
=\frac{1}{64a^2}\,8^{-(k+1)}.
$$

For the application, the support \(D=B_{2m}\cup E_m\cup F_m\) is exactly the support in accepted fact \(49bba4c121c43db7\): our active vector \(y\) is its active vector \(a\), our neutral vector \(t\) is its \(t\), and both use \(k=2m\). Its accepted convex-completeness and coordinate-budget assertions concern the support alone and therefore apply to every field. The predecessor uses the particular field \(\beta=0\); at \(\gamma=\eta=0\), the normalization in this packet is exactly its \(Z=|D|\), \(p_x=1/|D|\). For arbitrary \(\gamma,\eta\), the displayed \(Z\) and \(p\) are the original affine normalization on this same complete support, with no restriction inherited from that uniform specialization.

Every point of \(E_m\) has exactly two twos, every point of \(F_m\) exactly one, and all points of \(B_{2m}\) have none. Thus the disjoint core is \(D_1=B_{2m}\cup F_m\). For any fixed active two-index \(i\), there are \(2^{m-1}\) choices of the other active bits and \(\binom m{i+1}\) choices of the neutral vector. Therefore
$$
\begin{aligned}
|F_m|&=2^{m-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\binom m{i+1}
=2^{m-1}(2^m-m-1),\\
|D_1|&=2^{2m}+2^{m-1}(2^m-m-1)
<\frac32\,2^{2m}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Apply the max-two corollary with \(a=3/2\) and \(k=2m\). Since \(64(3/2)^2=144\), it gives both stated bounds for every \((\gamma,\eta)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m\).

For the final one-step refinement, let \(x\ne y\) be same-parity points in the stated complete one-step support and let \(c=(x+y)/2\). If \(c\) had a coordinate equal to two, both endpoints would have that coordinate equal to two. Their other coordinates would all be binary, so same parity would again force \(x=y\). Thus every such midpoint is Boolean, and completeness gives \(C_D\subseteq D\cap B_k\). Distinct points of \(D\cap B_k\) represent distinct occupied parity classes. Therefore \(r_D\le|D\cap B_k|\le q_D\). The generic theorem now gives both bounds \(1/(512q_D^3)\), without any missing-source or rank exception. Finally \(q_D\le2^k\) yields \(1/(512q_D^3)\ge(1/64)8^{-(k+1)}\), recovering the first-assertion moment bounds of accepted facts \(50c34c5bfb703ba9\) and \(b1d491a18220724d\) under the exact normalization maps given above.
statement:
Let \(k\ge1\) be an integer, and let \(D\subset\mathbb Z^k\) be finite and nonempty, with \(D=\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^k\). Set \(A=D\times\lbrace0\rbrace\subseteq\mathbb R^N\), where \(N=k+1\). For arbitrary \(\beta\in\mathbb R^k\), define the original weights, normalization, and probabilities by
$$
w_x=\exp(-\beta\cdot x),\qquad
Z=\sum_{x\in D}w_x,\qquad
p_{(x,0)}=\frac{w_x}{Z}\quad(x\in D).
$$
Write \(p_x=p_{(x,0)}\) solely as an abbreviation. For \(z\in A\), define its containing-closed-halfspace depth and original cubic moment by
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_p(z)&=\inf_{\substack{H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ closed affine halfspace}\\z\in H}}
\sum_{u\in A\cap H}p_u,\\
M_3(p)&=\sum_{z\in A}p_z\tau_p(z)^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
Halfspaces may be required to have nonzero normal. Allowing the whole space additionally leaves this infimum unchanged. For each \(c\in D\), define the full-reflection sum and its cubic by
$$
\begin{aligned}
s_p(c)&=\sum_{\substack{x,y\in D\\x+y=2c}}\min(p_x,p_y)
=\sum_{\substack{x\in D\\2c-x\in D}}\min(p_x,p_{2c-x}),\\
T(p)&=\sum_{c\in D}p_c\,s_p(c)^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
Thus \(s_p(c)\) counts ordered reflected pairs, with the diagonal pair \((c,c)\) once and each unordered distinct pair twice. Put
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal P_D&=\lbrace b\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^k:
\exists x\in D,\ x\equiv b\pmod2\rbrace,
&q_D&=|\mathcal P_D|,\\
C_D&=\left\lbrace\frac{x+y}{2}:x,y\in D,\ x\ne y,\ x\equiv y\pmod2\right\rbrace,
&r_D&=|C_D|.
\end{aligned}
$$
Completeness gives \(C_D\subseteq D\). The two bounds are
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac{1}{512\,q_D\max(q_D,r_D)^2},
\qquad
T(p)\ge\frac{1}{512\,q_D\max(q_D,r_D)^2}.
$$
They hold when \(r_D=0\) and for every affine rank of \(D\).

In particular, suppose additionally that \(B_k:=\lbrace0,1\rbrace^k\subseteq D\subseteq\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^k\), every point of \(D\) has at most two coordinates equal to two, and
$$
D_1:=\lbrace x\in D:\#\lbrace i:x_i=2\rbrace\le1\rbrace,
\qquad |D_1|\le a\,2^k\quad\text{for some real }a\ge1.
$$
Then \(q_D=2^k\), \(C_D\subseteq D_1\), and for every original field \(\beta\),
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac{1}{64a^2}\,8^{-(k+1)},
\qquad T(p)\ge\frac{1}{64a^2}\,8^{-(k+1)}.
$$
No paritywise star condition is imposed.

The application to accepted fact \(49bba4c121c43db7\) is as follows. Fix \(m\ge2\), put \(k=2m\), and write the active and neutral coordinate blocks as \((y,t)\), with \(y,t\in\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^m\). Here \(y\) is the vector denoted \(a\) in that fact. Let \(E_m\) consist of the points with one active two at index \(i\in\lbrace1,\ldots,m\rbrace\), one neutral two at index \(j\in\lbrace1,\ldots,m\rbrace\), and
$$
y_h\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace\ (h\ne i),\qquad
t_h\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace\ (h\ne j),\qquad
\sum_{h\ne j}t_h=i-1.
$$
Let \(F_m\) consist of the points with one active two at index \(i\in\lbrace1,\ldots,m-1\rbrace\), and
$$
y_h\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace\ (h\ne i),\qquad
t\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^m,\qquad
\sum_{h=1}^m t_h=i+1.
$$
For \(D=B_{2m}\cup E_m\cup F_m\), accepted fact \(49bba4c121c43db7\) establishes completeness and the at-most-two-twos property. For every pair of arbitrary vectors \(\gamma,\eta\in\mathbb R^m\), use the original field \(\beta=(\gamma,\eta)\), so that
$$
w_{(y,t)}=\exp(-\gamma\cdot y-\eta\cdot t),\qquad
Z=\sum_{(y,t)\in D}\exp(-\gamma\cdot y-\eta\cdot t),\qquad
p_{((y,t),0)}=\frac{\exp(-\gamma\cdot y-\eta\cdot t)}{Z}.
$$
These probabilities satisfy
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac1{144}\,8^{-(2m+1)},
\qquad T(p)\ge\frac1{144}\,8^{-(2m+1)}.
$$
In particular every active coefficient and every neutral coefficient may vary independently.

Finally, if a finite nonempty complete \(D\subseteq\lbrace0,1,2\rbrace^k\) has at most one two per point, without requiring any Boolean points to be present, then \(r_D\le q_D\). Consequently for every original field,
$$
M_3(p)\ge\frac1{512q_D^3},\qquad
T(p)\ge\frac1{512q_D^3}.
$$
Since \(q_D\le2^k\), this recovers the original-moment constants in accepted facts \(50c34c5bfb703ba9\) and \(b1d491a18220724d\), with the additional occupied-parity-count refinement.
